lead: A UPS keeps a load alive when the mains fails. Mains normally feeds a rectifier or charger, which holds a DC bus with a battery. An inverter turns that DC into AC for the load. In the on-line type the load always runs from the inverter, so a mains failure is invisible. UPS systems protect computers, hospital monitors, telecom towers, railway signalling and payment servers. This chapter compares off-line, line-interactive and on-line UPS topologies, explains transfer time, VA rating versus watts, output waveform quality, and battery sizing for a required backup time.
prereq: You need: switched-mode power supplies and the buck converter (DC-DC converters), and the full-bridge inverter with sinusoidal PWM (DC-AC inverters). The charger itself is in Battery chargers and emergency lighting.

blocks.text: An off-line UPS, also called standby, leaves the load on the mains in normal operation. The charger keeps the battery full and the inverter is off. When mains fails, a static transfer switch moves the load to the inverter. Transfer time is typically 4 to 10 ms, short enough for most computer power supplies to ride through. Some syllabi call this the standby type.

A line-interactive UPS adds a tap-changing transformer or buck-boost converter that corrects mains voltage while the load stays on the mains. The same inverter/charger charges the battery when mains is present. On mains failure it also switches the load to the inverter, with a transfer time of a few milliseconds, shorter than the off-line type because the inverter is already running and regulating. An on-line UPS, also called double conversion, rectifies the mains to a DC bus, holds a battery on that bus, and runs an inverter continuously into the load. The load never sees the mains directly. Mains failure changes the DC bus source from the charger to the battery, so there is no transfer time.

A static bypass is a fast switch, usually thyristors, from mains to load for inverter overload or fault. A maintenance bypass isolates the UPS for service. Ferro-resonant and rotary UPS exist for special cases; most data-centre UPS are on-line.

sections.h3: VA rating, waveform and battery sizing

blocks.text: UPS rating is in VA because inverter and transformer heating depends on current, and load current depends on apparent power S. Real power P = S × cos φ, where φ is the load power factor. A 1 kVA UPS with a 0.8 PF load can supply 800 W; with a 0.6 PF load it can supply only 600 W. Output THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + V₄² + …) ÷ V₁ × 100%, where V₁ is the fundamental RMS voltage and V₂, V₃, … are the harmonic RMS voltages. Below 3% is good for sensitive loads.
S = P / cos φ; Pdc = P / η; E = Vbat × Ah × DoD; t = E / Pdc

S is apparent power in VA; P is real load power in W; cos φ is load power factor; P<sub>dc</sub> is battery-side DC power in W; η is inverter efficiency; V<sub>bat</sub> is nominal battery voltage in V; Ah is battery capacity in ampere-hours; DoD is depth of discharge as a fraction; E is usable energy in Wh; t is backup time in hours.

Battery sizing uses usable energy, not the printed Ah alone. The charger must also replace the energy taken during an outage. Ageing, low temperature and high discharge current reduce the delivered Ah, so field designs add margin. Grid-scale battery interfaces are in Renewable energy and battery storage interfacing.

A linear supply steps down and rectifies the mains, then drops the excess voltage across a series transistor; it is clean but bulky and low efficiency. An SMPS chops at high frequency, so it is small and efficient, but it draws pulsed current with high crest factor and injects harmonics. Crest factor is the peak value divided by the RMS value: about 1.41 for a sine, often 2.5 to 3 for an SMPS. That crest factor is what matters for UPS sizing: the UPS must supply the peak current of the SMPS load without clipping or tripping. A UPS is an AC power supply with stored energy. It also acts as a power conditioner, regulating voltage, filtering spikes and holding frequency. A power conditioner may only filter and regulate, with no battery. Choose UPS VA from load VA, not watts alone, and add margin for startup.

examples.question: A 1 kVA on-line UPS feeds a 640 W load at 0.8 lagging power factor. The battery is 48 V, 100 Ah, the inverter efficiency is 90%, and the battery may be taken down to 80% of its capacity. Find the DC current drawn from the battery and the backup time.
steps: Load apparent power: S = P / cos φ = 640 / 0.8 = 800 VA. The 1 kVA UPS rating is greater than 800 VA, so the load fits.
Inverter DC power: P<sub>dc</sub> = P / η = 640 / 0.9 = 711.1 W.
Battery DC current: I = P<sub>dc</sub> / V<sub>bat</sub> = 711.1 / 48 = 14.8 A.
Usable battery energy: E = V<sub>bat</sub> × Ah × DoD = 48 × 100 × 0.8 = 3840 Wh.
Backup time: t = E / P<sub>dc</sub> = 3840 / 711.1 = 5.40 h, about 5 h 24 min. Check: 14.8 A × 5.40 h = 80 Ah, which is 80 % of the 100 Ah battery, as allowed.
examples.answer: The battery supplies about 14.8 A at 48 V, and the usable energy gives about 5.4 hours of backup.

W = 640.0
pf = 0.8
eta = 0.9
V = 48.0
Ah = 100.0
dod = 0.8
S = W / pf
Pdc = W / eta
I = Pdc / V
E = V * Ah * dod
t = E / Pdc
print(f'{S:.2f}')
print(f'{Pdc:.2f}')
print(f'{I:.2f}')
print(f'{E:.2f}')
print(f'{t:.2f}')

examples.question: A server room needs 30 minutes of backup for a 2 kVA load at 0.8 power factor. The on-line UPS has a 96 V battery string (eight 12 V blocks in series), the inverter efficiency is 92 %, the battery may be discharged to 80 %, and the designer adds 25 % for ageing. The maker's table says a block gives only 60 % of its 20-hour Ah rating when it is emptied in 30 minutes. Find the battery current and the Ah rating of each block.
steps: Real power: P = S × cos φ = 2000 × 0.8 = 1600 W.
DC power from the battery: P<sub>dc</sub> = P / η = 1600 / 0.92 = 1739.1 W. Battery current at 96 V: I = 1739.1 / 96 = 18.1 A.
Energy for 30 minutes: 1739.1 W × 0.5 h = 869.6 Wh.
Allow for depth of discharge: 869.6 / 0.8 = 1087.0 Wh. Add 25 % for ageing: 1087.0 × 1.25 = 1358.7 Wh.
Ah at the 30-minute rate: 1358.7 Wh / 96 V = 14.15 Ah.
Convert to the 20-hour rating printed on the block: 14.15 / 0.60 = 23.6 Ah. The next standard size is 26 Ah.
examples.answer: The battery supplies 18.1 A; use eight 12 V blocks of at least 23.6 Ah (20-hour rating), so 12 V, 26 Ah blocks.
examples.check:
P=2000*0.8
Pdc=P/0.92
I=Pdc/96
E=Pdc*0.5
E2=E/0.8*1.25
Ah=E2/96
print(round(Pdc,1),round(I,1),round(E,1),round(E2,1),round(Ah,2),round(Ah/0.6,1))

traps: Multiplying VA by hours and calling it stored energy. Apparent power must pass through the load power factor and the inverter efficiency before it becomes battery watts.
Using battery Ah × voltage as backup time without depth of discharge and inverter efficiency. A 100 Ah battery is not 100 Ah of usable energy.
Choosing a UPS only by watts. The UPS VA rating must exceed load VA, because current heats the inverter and transformer.
Thinking every UPS has the same transfer time. Off-line and line-interactive types switch the load; on-line double conversion does not transfer the load on mains failure.
Forgetting that a lead-acid block delivers fewer Ah at a high rate. A 30-minute UPS discharge gets only a part of the 20-hour Ah printed on the block, so use the maker's table.

quiz.a: An uninterruptible power supply is an AC backup system with a charger, a battery and an inverter. It feeds the load when mains fails.

quiz.q: Why does an on-line UPS have no transfer time on mains failure?
quiz.a: The load always runs from the inverter. Mains failure only changes the DC bus source from the charger to the battery, so the output AC does not switch path.

quiz.q: A 1500 VA UPS feeds a 900 W load at 0.75 power factor. Is the load within the VA rating?
quiz.a: S = P / cos φ = 900 / 0.75 = 1200 VA. 1200 VA is less than 1500 VA, so the load is within rating, with 300 VA margin.

quiz.q: A 48 V, 100 Ah battery is used to 80% depth of discharge. Inverter efficiency is 90% and the load is 500 W. Find the backup time.
Why can a 1000 VA UPS trip on a 600 W SMPS load?
quiz.a: The SMPS draws current in narrow peaks, so its crest factor is high and its RMS current may exceed the sine-wave rating. The UPS must supply the peak current, and protection may trip even when average watts look small.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a static bypass and a maintenance bypass?
quiz.a: A static bypass automatically connects the load to mains during inverter overload or fault. A maintenance bypass is a manual path that isolates the UPS so it can be serviced.

quiz.q: A battery falls from 48 V to 42 V near the end of discharge while supplying the same load. What happens to battery current?
quiz.a: For the same DC power, I = P<sub>dc</sub> / V<sub>bat</sub>. At 42 V the current is 48/42 = 1.14 times the current at 48 V, about 14% higher. More current means more internal loss and a faster voltage fall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern UPS designs use lithium-ion batteries, high-efficiency SiC inverters, modular parallel units and an "eco mode" that runs on the bypass and switches to double conversion only when the mains misbehaves. Data-centre UPS may coordinate with generators, solar and battery storage. Search next for double conversion UPS, static transfer switch, depth of discharge and IEC 62040.
